content: Geology, derived from the Greek words ge (meaning the earth) and logos (meaning word or reason), is the scientific study of the Earth. This field encompasses the Earth's composition, structure, physical properties, history, and the dynamic processes that shape it. The Earth is approximately 5 billion years old, and its tectonic plates move over a viscous mantle, forming the Earth's crust. Geologists play a critical role in locating and managing natural resources, such as oil. The principles of geology are also applied to other celestial bodies in the solar system, a field known as astrogeology. The term geology was first used by Jean-André Deluc in 1778 and was formally introduced as a fixed term by Horace-Bénédict de Saussure in 1779. History of Geology Georg Agricola (1494–1555) authored the first systematic treatise on mining and smelting, titled De re metallica libri XII, which included an appendix called Buch von den Lebewesen unter Tage (Book of the Creatures Beneath the Earth). This work, published in 1556, covered topics such as wind energy, hydrodynamic power, melting furnaces, ore transportation, the extraction of substances like soda, sulfur, and alum, as well as administrative issues related to mining. James Hutton is often regarded as the first modern geologist. In 1785, he presented a paper titled Theory of the Earth to the Royal Society of Edinburgh. In this work, Hutton proposed that the Earth must be significantly older than previously thought to allow sufficient time for mountains to erode, sediments to form new rocks at the bottom of the sea, and these rocks to be uplifted to form new land. Hutton's followers, known as Plutonists, believed that some rocks were formed through volcanic activity (vulcanism), in contrast to the Neptunists, who argued that all rocks had precipitated from a large ocean that gradually receded over time. William Smith (1769–1839) created some of the earliest geological maps and pioneered the process of ordering rock strata by studying the fossils they contained. Sir Charles Lyell, in 1830, published his influential book Principles of Geology, which he continued to revise until his death in 1875. Lyell championed the doctrine of uniformitarianism, which posits that slow geological processes have occurred consistently throughout Earth's history and continue to do so today. This theory stood in contrast to catastrophism, which suggested that Earth's features were formed by singular, catastrophic events that left the planet unchanged thereafter. Although Hutton supported uniformitarianism, it was not widely accepted during his time. The theory of continental drift was proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912 and later supported by Arthur Holmes. However, it did not gain widespread acceptance until the 1960s, when the theory of plate tectonics was developed. Fields and Sub-disciplines of Geology Geology encompasses numerous specialized fields, including: Economic geology Environmental geology Geochemistry Geochronology Geodesy Geomicrobiology Geomorphology Geophysics Glaciology Hydrogeology (or geohydrology) Marine geology Mineralogy Paleoclimatology Paleontology Pedology (soil study) Petroleum geology Petrology Sedimentology Seismology Stratigraphy Structural geology Tectonics Volcanology Additionally, there is engineering geology, which supports civil engineering projects, particularly in geotechnical engineering and geological engineering. It is important to note the distinction between geological engineering and engineering geology: geological engineers are licensed as engineers, while engineering geologists are licensed as geologists.
